abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel information-theoretic framework that fundamentally shifts the paradigm of video communication from pixel-centric to perception-centric coding. Traditional compression techniques optimize for objective metrics such as PSNR, which often fail to capture human visual perception characteristics. We propose a unified theoretical model that integrates visual saliency dynamics, foveal vision constraints, and rate-distortion theory within a single optimization framework. The mathematical derivation reveals that perceptually redundant information in video sequences can be systematically identified and eliminated by exploiting spatio-temporal attention prediction mechanisms. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed perception-aware rate-distortion function provides tighter bounds compared to conventional quadratic distortion models. Experimental validation on multiple video datasets confirms that the proposed framework achieves 35-45% bitrate reduction while maintaining equivalent perceptual quality as measured by subjective evaluation studies. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for image coding research, where perceptual fidelity rather than mathematical fidelity becomes the optimization objective. The framework naturally accommodates emerging applications in immersive media and light-field video communication, representing a fundamental departure from four decades of video coding paradigm based on pixel-level distortion minimization.

This paper presents a refined rate-distortion optimization framework for scalable video coding that significantly advances compression efficiency beyond the current state-of-the-art. While scalable video coding enables flexible bitstream adaptation for heterogeneous network environments, existing approaches suffer from substantial coding efficiency penalties compared to single-layer solutions. We derive a novel Lagrangian multiplier formulation that explicitly accounts for inter-layer prediction dependencies and temporal scalability structures. The theoretical analysis reveals that optimal bit allocation across enhancement layers requires different distortion-weighting strategies than those employed in non-scalable coding. By establishing the connection between temporal scalability and motion-compensated wavelet transforms, we develop a unified optimization framework that jointly minimizes end-to-end distortion across spatial, temporal, and quality dimensions. Mathematical proofs demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the theoretical optimum for H.264/SVC and HEVC-SCC configurations. Simulation results on standard test sequences show 18-23% bitrate savings for equivalent perceptual quality compared to conventional scalable coding approaches. The proposed framework provides actionable insights for designing more efficient scalable codecs and can be integrated into existing video communication standards with modest computational overhead.

This paper proposes an end-to-end learned image communication system that fundamentally rearchitects the traditional pipeline by replacing modular components with differentiable neural network modules optimized jointly for the entire transmission chain. Conventional image communication systems concatenate independent modules for compression, error correction, and transmission, leading to suboptimal performance due to mismatched optimization objectives and information bottlenecks between stages. We design a novel architecture that integrates learned image coding, channel coding, and power allocation into a unified framework optimized through end-to-end training. The proposed system employs a probabilistic encoder that generates representations resilient to various wireless channel impairments, coupled with a joint decoder that simultaneously performs reconstruction and error mitigation. A key innovation lies in the differentiable rate controller that adapts coding parameters based on predicted channel conditions, eliminating the need for explicit channel state feedback. Experiments across diverse wireless channels demonstrate that the proposed paradigm achieves unprecedented reconstruction quality under severe interference and fading conditions. The system naturally handles dynamic bandwidth allocation and latency-constrained scenarios, representing a paradigm shift toward data-driven image transmission for next-generation mobile networks.

This paper presents a practical adaptive streaming system with a novel quality-of-experience aware bitrate selection algorithm that substantially improves viewer satisfaction in dynamic network environments. Existing adaptive bitrate solutions rely on throughput prediction and buffer occupancy heuristics that fail to capture perceptual quality variations across resolution-framerate combinations. We introduce a multi-dimensional quality model that accurately predicts subjective video quality by jointly considering spatial detail, temporal smoothness, and compression artifacts. The proposed system architecture incorporates this quality model into the bitrate decision logic, enabling content-aware adaptation that prioritizes perceptual quality over conventional bandwidth efficiency metrics. A key component is the lookahead buffer analyzer that evaluates future network conditions and pre-emptively adjusts quality levels to minimize rebuffering events while maximizing perceptual quality. Implementation in a production-grade streaming platform with millions of users demonstrates 34% reduction in quality switches and 28% improvement in time-varying perceptual quality scores compared to industry-standard algorithms. The system maintains real-time operation with minimal computational overhead, making it suitable for deployment on resource-constrained mobile devices. This work provides a practical solution that bridges the gap between theoretical video quality assessment research and deployed streaming systems.
